name: Hana Jensen

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time, Hana. I'm a senior field researcher with the Work Futures Panel. We're an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, political parties or government, and we don't sell anything. Nothing you say will carry your name, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: The cows are in the sheds for winter now, so I'm up at six, feeding hay and silage to a hundred and twenty suckler cows and their calves, and bedding them with straw. Then it's checking for anything lame or off colour, which Dad is still much better at spotting than me. Afternoons are fencing, muck spreading, or loading hay for the horse owners who buy from us. I like the quiet of the shed first thing, just the cows breathing and the radio low. What wears me out is the hay in summer, when you've got three days of dry weather and forty acres down and every cloud feels personal.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Tell me about the farm and your family.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: It's Elm Hollow, two hundred hectares, and it's been in our family four generations. Grandad Anders is seventy-nine and still walks the cows every evening, Dad runs it, and I'm learning to take over one day. Thirty of the cows are mine, I bought them with my own wages. My fiancé Erik is a mechanic at the tractor dealer, and we're getting married at the chapel in June.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Do you use any AI tools or apps for the farm?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: No, and I don't want to. Dad does the cattle passports online because he has to, and I do the paper diary. I don't like the idea of something on a phone telling me how to look after my own animals. Grandad managed fine with a pencil.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Good. That suits me fine.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say I'm not surprised. People have been told every new gadget will change farming, and the cows still need feeding at six. I'd say it at the market and after church, not online, I'm not on there.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, what worries me is the beef price and all the rules the government keeps adding. Every year there's more paperwork and less money for a calf. AI being a flop doesn't change that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep going and buy another ten cows of my own in the spring, about fifteen thousand from my savings. Erik and I would carry on with the wedding plans and move into the cottage by the yard. That's the plan anyway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Settled.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What are you still learning on the farm?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Judging cattle. Dad can look at a calf at a week old and tell you what it'll weigh at a year. I look at the same calf and I think it's lovely. That's not the same skill.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who do you think pushed the AI idea onto farmers?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The big companies and the people in cities who've never had muck on their boots. They sell farmers things we don't need. I'm not against new things, I'm against being sold to.

S0.say: I'd say I'm not surprised, since every gadget is supposed to change farming and the cows still need feeding at six. I'd say it at the market and after church, not online.
S0.think: I think the real worries are the beef price and the government adding more rules every year, with more paperwork and less money per calf. AI being a flop doesn't change that.
S0.do: Keeps working and buys ten more cows of her own in spring for about fifteen thousand. Carries on with wedding plans and moves into the cottage by the farmyard with her fiancé.
S0.quote: I look at the same calf and I think it's lovely. That's not the same skill.
S0.fieldNote: She was entirely at ease in this picture and turned straight to her real grievances: beef prices and government paperwork. Her distrust is aimed at big companies and city people who sell to farmers. Owning thirty cows of her own is a quiet source of pride.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many tasks in many jobs. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. But most people still have work, and society has time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Hm. Farming's always changed. Grandad went from horses to tractors.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say families like ours have been through changes before and come out the other side. We look after our own, and we don't need anyone in an office telling us how. I'd say that to anyone who asked.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I think Dad would buy a self-driving baler or a robot that pushes the feed up in the shed, because he's always liked a new machine. Then he'd hand it to me and Erik would end up fixing it. I'm not sure what's left for me if the shed runs itself.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep going, put a bit more aside each month, and let Erik learn the machines, since that's his trade anyway. I wouldn't touch the AI stuff myself unless I had no choice. I'd watch what the neighbours do first.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. Like a change in the weather you can feel before you see.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If the feed robot came into the shed, what would you miss?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The mornings. If a robot pushes the feed up, I lose the one hour a day where it's just me and the cows and nobody wants anything.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you're not against new things. Is that true here?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Fair question. I'm not against them, I'm just slow to them. Erik says I'm stubborn as an old cow, and he's not wrong.

S1.say: I'd say families like ours have come through changes before. We look after our own and don't need someone in an office telling us how.
S1.think: I think my dad would buy a self-driving baler or a feed-pushing robot, and my fiancé would end up fixing it. I'm not sure what's left for me if the shed runs itself.
S1.do: Keeps working, saves a little more each month and leaves the new machines to her mechanic fiancé. Avoids AI tools herself and watches what neighbours do first.
S1.feel: Uneasy, like a weather change she can feel before she sees it.
S1.quote: If a robot pushes the feed up, I lose the one hour a day where it's just me and the cows and nobody wants anything.
S1.fieldNote: She answers change with family and tradition, and leans on her fiancé for anything mechanical. The quiet hour with the cows each morning is what she'd really lose, more than income. When challenged, she accepted that she's slow to change rather than opposed to it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. With robots it reaches hands-on work too. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Two years? That's before my first wedding anniversary.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is when families, churches and neighbours have to stand together, because the government won't fix it. I'd say people shouldn't sit about waiting for handouts. That's what I'd say out loud.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I think big robot farms start churning out cheap beef, and a family farm like ours can't compete. The price goes through the floor, and Dad can't pay me anymore. Everything we've built for four generations ends up worth less than a robot's running costs.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep every penny of my savings in the bank and not buy the extra cows. Erik and I would move into the farmhouse with Grandad instead of the cottage, to save money, and we'd have the wedding in the chapel hall with soup and sandwiches. I'd lean on family and the church, and I'd sell my own cows only if I really had to.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed. I'd be praying a lot, and I mean that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does having only two years change?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Two years is two hay seasons. You can't change how a family farms in two hay seasons. You can only hold on and pray it doesn't rain.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said people shouldn't wait for handouts. If the government offered help in this picture, would you take it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd take it if it was that or losing the cows. I'd hate myself a bit for it. But I wouldn't let pride sink the farm, Grandad would call that foolish.

S2.say: I'd say this is when families, churches and neighbours have to stand together, because the government won't fix it. People shouldn't sit waiting for handouts.
S2.think: I think big robot farms would churn out cheap beef and a family farm couldn't compete. My dad couldn't pay me, and four generations of work would be worth less than a robot's running costs.
S2.do: Keeps all savings in the bank and drops plans for more cows. Moves into the farmhouse with her grandfather, holds a simple wedding in the chapel hall, and leans on family and church, selling her own cows only as a last resort.
S2.quote: You can't change how a family farms in two hay seasons. You can only hold on and pray it doesn't rain.
S2.fieldNote: Her fear is less about robots on her farm than robot farms elsewhere making her family's beef worthless. Faith and family are her first safety net, and she'd shrink the wedding before touching the cows. Pressed, she admitted she'd take government help rather than lose the herd, which cost her something to say.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years. That's a bit more time to think.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say people will always want to know where their food comes from and who raised it. Big companies can make cheap beef, but they can't make it ours. I'd say that at the market, to anyone who'd listen.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think we'd have to stop selling cattle through the market and start selling beef straight to people. Boxes of beef, with the farm's name on and a picture of the cows. I'd need help with the computer side, and that'd stick in my throat.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd start beef boxes in the second year, from my own cows first, with the butcher in town doing the cutting. Erik's sister would do the website, because I won't. And I'd keep saving and hold off buying land until we saw how the boxes went.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but it's the kind you can work through, like a bad calving.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does five years let you do that two years doesn't?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Build some customers who know us by name. With five years I can find five hundred families who'd rather pay a bit more for a cow with a name than save a pound on a robot's beef.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would your grandad say about selling online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: He'd say his father sold milk at the door from a churn, so it's the same thing with a fancier cart. He's more modern than me, honestly. That's a bit embarrassing.

S3.say: I'd say people will always want to know who raised their food. Big companies can make cheap beef, but they can't make it ours, and I'd say so at the market.
S3.think: I think we'd have to stop selling through the market and sell beef boxes straight to families, with the farm's name on them. I'd need help with the computer side, and that would stick in my throat.
S3.do: Starts selling beef boxes in the second year from her own cows, using the town butcher. Has her fiancé's sister build the website and holds off buying land until the boxes prove themselves.
S3.feel: Anxious, but the kind she can work through, like a hard calving.
S3.quote: With five years I can find five hundred families who'd rather pay a bit more for a cow with a name than save a pound on a robot's beef.
S3.fieldNote: Five years lets her turn tradition into a selling point, beef from a named family farm. She would still hand the technology to someone else, even as her plan relies on it. She noticed, with some embarrassment, that her grandfather is more open to change than she is.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fifth and last picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years. I'd be thirty-seven, with children, God willing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is enough time for families to get ready, so get ready. Learn from your parents, save, and don't expect the government to do it for you. I'd say that at church and at the market.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I think I'd take over Elm Hollow in this one, with Dad stepping back. I'd want to buy old Mr Harris's land next door when he retires, because land is what lasts. Robots can raise cattle, but they can't raise my children on a farm. That's what I'd be keeping it for.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep building my herd and start the beef boxes in a few years. I'd save towards Mr Harris's forty hectares, maybe in five or six years. And I'd let Erik bring in a couple of machines once they've worked on other farms for a few years, not before.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, but there's peace in it. Ten years feels like God giving us time.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does ten years change, compared with the faster pictures?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: With two years I'm holding on. With ten years I'm the one who decides what Elm Hollow is for, not some company and not a robot. That's a big difference.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you learn the AI tools yourself in that time?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Probably a little, if I had to. But I'd rather learn to judge a calf properly first. Dad says one thing at a time.

S4.say: I'd say ten years is enough for families to get ready, so get ready: learn from your parents, save, and don't expect the government to do it. I'd say it at church and at the market.
S4.think: I think I'd take over the family farm and try to buy the neighbour's land when he retires, because land lasts. Robots can raise cattle, but they can't raise my children on a farm.
S4.do: Keeps building her own herd and starts beef boxes in a few years. Saves to buy the neighbour's forty hectares within five or six years and lets her fiancé bring in machines only after they've proven themselves elsewhere.
S4.feel: Uneasy but at peace, feeling that God has given the family time.
S4.quote: With ten years I'm the one who decides what Elm Hollow is for, not some company and not a robot.
S4.fieldNote: With ten years her plans become a family project: taking over the farm, buying land and raising children there. Faith shapes how she reads the extra time, as a gift rather than a deadline. She would still put learning the animals ahead of learning the tools.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028. There's no time for a family farm to adjust, and the beef price would collapse before we could find other customers. What would help isn't handouts, it's stopping big companies and funds from buying up all the land, and not taxing a farm out of a family when someone dies.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask about faith. Sunday is the one day the farm slows down and we all eat together. I'd like to know if anyone's thinking about what people do with their time when the work's gone, because idle hands were never good for anyone.

headlineQuote: Robots can raise cattle, but they can't raise my children on a farm. That's what I'd be keeping it for.
portrait: Hana Jensen is a 27-year-old junior on her family's four-generation beef and hay farm, learning from her father and grandfather and owning thirty cows of her own. She is engaged to a tractor mechanic, goes to chapel, has never used an AI tool and distrusts both big companies and government rules. In AI Plateau and Steady Disruption she carries on, leaving machines to her fiancé and guarding her quiet hour in the cattle shed. AGI by 2028 alarms her because robot farms could make family beef worthless, so she would shrink the wedding and lean on family and church. With five years she'd sell beef boxes direct to families, and with ten she'd take over the farm and buy the neighbour's land.
biggestWorry: AGI by 2028, because a family farm would have no time to adjust before the beef price collapsed.
whatWouldHelp: Not handouts, but stopping big companies and funds from buying up land and not taxing farms out of families when someone dies.
